hook: A delivery company promises 30 minutes on average. A manager thinks it is longer. Before anyone computes a number, the test has to be set up: which parameter, which hypotheses, which direction, and whether the conditions let a t procedure be trusted. Most lost points on inference questions happen here, not in the arithmetic.

prereq.q: Which pair of hypotheses is written correctly?
options: $H_0: p = 0.56$, $H_a: p > 0.56$, using the sample result
prereq.why: Hypotheses are about the parameter, the null holds the equals sign, and the null value comes from the question.

prereq.q: For paired data, a confidence interval for the mean difference is built from
options: the differences within each pair, as one sample
the two groups as separate samples
the larger of the two means
prereq.why: Subtract within each pair, then use a one-sample t procedure on the differences.

figure.caption: Resting heart rates of 12 gym members before and after a breathing class, joined by a line for each member, and the dotplot of the 12 differences (before minus after). The test uses the differences.

chain.cause: Start from the question, before the data
chain.effect: it gives the parameter, the hypothesized mean $\mu_0$ and the direction of $H_a$
define $\mu$ in context: "the true mean ... of all ..."

chain.cause: If each individual gives two linked measurements
chain.effect: the data are paired: test $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ on the differences, with the order of subtraction stated

chain.cause: Check random, 10% and normal/large sample in words
chain.effect: a one-sample (or paired) t test can be trusted, with $\text{df} = n - 1$

ideas: Paired t test: a one-sample t test on the differences, $H_0: \mu_d = 0$. The order of subtraction sets the direction of $H_a$.
Hypotheses use parameters ($\mu$, $\mu_d$), never statistics ($\bar{x}$), and the direction comes from the question, never from the sample result.
Conditions: random; 10% when sampling without replacement; normal population, $n \ge 30$, or a graph of the sample (or the differences) without strong skew or outliers.

misconception.wrong: The sample mean was below 30, so the alternative should be $H_a: \mu < 30$.
misconception.right: The alternative comes from the research question asked before the data. If the question is "different from 30", the alternative is $\mu \ne 30$ whatever the sample shows.

summary: To set up a t test for a mean, name the parameter in context, write $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ and an alternative whose direction comes from the question, and check random, 10% and normal/large sample. For paired data, test the mean difference $\mu_d$ with a paired t test on the differences, saying which way you subtracted.
